Azure Virtual Network and Subnets: Concepts and Step-by-Step Creation

Every VM, private endpoint and database you deploy in Azure lands in a VNet. This post covers what a VNet and a subnet are, how to plan their address ranges, and how to build one with two subnets in the portal.

By Nithin Sunke · November 2026 · ~10 min read
In this post
  1. What is an Azure Virtual Network?
  2. What is a subnet?
  3. Planning the address space
  4. Creating the VNet and subnets in the portal
  5. The same build with Azure CLI
  6. Limits and gotchas
  7. Azure vs OCI quick map

1. What is an Azure Virtual Network?

An Azure Virtual Network (VNet) is your own private, isolated network inside Azure. It works like the network in your on-prem data centre: you choose the private IP ranges, split them into subnets, and control how traffic moves in and out. Because it runs on Azure, you also get Azure's scale, availability and isolation.

Some key properties:

  • Regional. A VNet lives in one region, for example Central India, but it spans all availability zones in that region.
  • Isolated by default. Resources in one VNet cannot reach another VNet until you connect them with peering or a VPN.
  • Address space. You define one or more CIDR ranges, usually from private RFC 1918 space such as 10.0.0.0/16.
  • Free. The VNet and its subnets cost nothing. You pay for what you attach, such as public IPs, NAT gateways, Bastion, Firewall and peering traffic.
  • Built-in DNS. By default, Azure-provided DNS resolves names inside the VNet. You can switch to custom DNS servers later.

2. What is a subnet?

A subnet is a slice of the VNet's address space. Every resource that needs a private IP, such as a VM NIC or a private endpoint, is placed in a subnet and receives an IP from that subnet's range.

Subnets are how you separate tiers. In this lab, the application servers go in app-sn and the databases go in db-sn, so each tier can have its own security rules.

The following can be attached per subnet:

  • Network Security Group (NSG): allow and deny rules for inbound and outbound traffic.
  • Route table (UDR): custom routes, for example sending all traffic through a firewall.
  • NAT gateway: controlled outbound internet access.
  • Service endpoints and delegations: optimised access to PaaS services, or dedicating the subnet to a service such as SQL Managed Instance.
Azure reserves 5 IPs in every subnet The network address, the first three host addresses (default gateway and two for Azure DNS) and the broadcast address cannot be used. In 10.0.1.0/26, that means .0, .1, .2, .3 and .63, so your first VM gets 10.0.1.4.

Private subnets (no default outbound access)

Historically, a VM in Azure could reach the internet even with no public IP, through hidden "default outbound access". Microsoft is retiring this. When you create a subnet in the portal you now see "Enable private subnet (no default outbound access)", and the portal notes that after March 31, 2026, private subnet will be the default for new virtual networks.

In a private subnet, a VM has no internet access unless you give it one explicitly, with a NAT gateway (recommended), a public IP, or a load balancer outbound rule. This is more secure, but remember it when apt update or Windows activation fails on a fresh VM.

3. Planning the address space

Planning first saves you from re-creating networks later. Address ranges are hard to change once resources are deployed.

  • Don't overlap. Pick a range that doesn't clash with on-prem or other VNets you may peer with later. Overlapping VNets cannot be peered.
  • Go big on the VNet, right-size the subnets. A /16 VNet gives room to add subnets later. Each subnet only needs enough for its tier plus growth.
  • Smallest subnet is /29, which is 8 IPs with 3 usable. Some services need more. For example, GatewaySubnet should be /27 or larger, and AzureBastionSubnet needs at least /26.
  • Leave gaps. Placing db-sn at 10.0.1.0 rather than right after app-sn keeps tidy, readable boundaries.

Design used in this lab:

ItemValueNotes
Resource groupcenteralindiaExisting RG used for the lab
RegionCentral IndiaClosest region (Pune)
VNetlab-vnet10.0.0.0/16, 65,536 addresses
Subnet 1app-sn10.0.0.0/24, range 10.0.0.0 – 10.0.0.255
Subnet 2db-sn10.0.1.0/26, range 10.0.1.0 – 10.0.1.63
Private subnetEnabled on bothNo default outbound internet

4. Creating the VNet and subnets in the portal

1

Start from "Create a resource"

Sign in to the Azure portal. On the home page, click Create a resource.

2

Open All services

Virtual network isn't in the popular list, so click All services under Explore more.

3

Networking → Virtual network

In the left category list, choose Networking (1). Under Network foundation, hover over Virtual network (2) and click Create, or click the name to open the list view.

Tip: typing "virtual networks" in the top search bar gets you here faster.

4

Click Create

The Virtual networks list is empty because this is a fresh subscription. Click + Create.

5

Basics tab: project and instance details

  • Subscription: your subscription (here, Azure subscription 1).
  • Resource group: select an existing one, or click Create new. This lab uses centeralindia.
  • Virtual network name: lab-vnet.
  • Region: (Asia Pacific) Central India.

Click Next.

Security tab The next tab offers Azure Bastion, Azure Firewall and DDoS Network Protection. Leave all three disabled for a learning lab, because each adds hourly cost. You can add them to the VNet later.
6

Address space tab: review the default

Azure proposes 10.0.0.0/16 with a subnet called default (10.0.0.0/24). The /16 works for this lab, so keep it. Click the pencil (edit) icon on the default subnet and rename it to app-sn. Keep the range 10.0.0.0/24 and tick Enable private subnet.

7

Add the database subnet

Click + Add a subnet and fill in:

  • Subnet purpose: Default
  • Name: db-sn
  • IPv4 address range: 10.0.0.0/16 (the VNet's space)
  • Starting address: 10.0.1.0
  • Size: /26 (64 addresses). The portal shows the range as 10.0.1.0 – 10.0.1.63.
  • Enable private subnet: ticked
  • NAT gateway / NSG / Route table: None for now. We'll attach an NSG in a later lab.

Click Add.

8

Confirm both subnets

The address space now shows two subnets: app-sn (10.0.0.0/24, 256 addresses) and db-sn (10.0.1.0/26, 64 addresses). Skip Tags, or add env=lab, then go to Review + create.

9

Review + create

Wait for Validation passed, check the summary (Bastion, Firewall and DDoS disabled; both subnets private), and click Create.

Tip: View automation template shows the ARM JSON for exactly what you configured. It's a good way to start learning infrastructure as code.

10

Deployment complete

Deployment takes a few seconds. When you see Your deployment is complete, click Go to resource.

11

Verify the VNet

The overview confirms the resource group, the location (Central India), the address space 10.0.0.0/16 and 2 subnets, with Azure-provided DNS. The Capabilities tab lists optional add-ons (DDoS protection, Azure Firewall, Peerings, Defender for Cloud, Private endpoints), all Not configured for now.

Click Settings → Subnets in the left menu to see each subnet's range and available IP count. app-sn shows 251 available and db-sn shows 59, because of the 5 reserved IPs.

5. The same build with Azure CLI

Once you understand the portal screens, the CLI is faster to repeat. Run this in Cloud Shell (Bash):

RG=centeralindia
LOC=centralindia

# Resource group (skip if it already exists)
az group create -n $RG -l $LOC

# VNet with the first subnet
az network vnet create -g $RG -n lab-vnet -l $LOC \
  --address-prefixes 10.0.0.0/16 \
  --subnet-name app-sn --subnet-prefixes 10.0.0.0/24

# Second subnet
az network vnet subnet create -g $RG --vnet-name lab-vnet \
  -n db-sn --address-prefixes 10.0.1.0/26

# Make both subnets private (no default outbound access)
for s in app-sn db-sn; do
  az network vnet subnet update -g $RG --vnet-name lab-vnet -n $s \
    --default-outbound-access false
done

# Verify
az network vnet subnet list -g $RG --vnet-name lab-vnet \
  --query "[].{name:name, prefix:addressPrefix, private:defaultOutboundAccess}" -o table

6. Limits and gotchas

  • One region per VNet. To connect regions, use global VNet peering.
  • A subnet can't be resized while it holds resources. Size for growth up front.
  • Subnets can't overlap each other, and they must fit inside the VNet's address space.
  • VNet address space can be extended. You can add another range, such as 10.1.0.0/16, later, even with peering in place.
  • A resource's NIC stays in its subnet. To move a VM to another VNet you must redeploy it. Moving it to another subnet in the same VNet is allowed.
  • Default quotas are generous: about 1,000 VNets per subscription per region and up to 3,000 subnets per VNet.

7. Azure vs OCI quick map

If you're coming from Oracle Cloud like me, this mapping helps:

AzureOCIDifference
Virtual Network (VNet)VCNBoth regional. An Azure VNet spans all AZs; OCI VCN spans all ADs.
SubnetSubnetAzure subnets are always regional. OCI subnets can be regional or AD-specific.
Private subnetPrivate subnetOCI blocks public IPs; Azure blocks implicit outbound access.
NSG on subnetSecurity listAzure NSG rules have priorities; OCI security lists don't.
NSG on NICNetwork Security GroupSimilar per-VNIC model.
Implicit system routesInternet gatewayAzure has no separate IGW resource.
NAT gatewayNAT gatewaySame purpose.
Route table (UDR)Route tableSame concept.

What's next

The network is ready. In the next lab I'll create an NSG, attach it to app-sn, and deploy a Linux VM into the subnet. Then I'll add a NAT gateway so the VM can reach the internet from a private subnet.

Cleanup: an empty VNet costs nothing, so you can keep it for the next lab. To remove it: az network vnet delete -g centeralindia -n lab-vnet.
